column2: The following evening.
“Hey, Old Tang. Do you know what they ask in American college interviews?” Lu Mingfei typed on QQ.
“What? You got an interview?” Old Tang’s panda avatar bounced frantically.

Old Tang was the only person Lu Mingfei could think of who might help. He lived in New York and was Chinese American. His last name was probably Tang. Everyone called him Old Tang, though he wasn’t particularly old. Apparently, he had grown up in America, so his spoken Chinese wasn’t very fluent, but he managed well enough typing online. Apart from occasionally thinking a little too highly of himself, Old Tang had no serious faults. His ambition in life was to become Indiana Jones.
“Yeah. Tomorrow morning. I’ve searched all over the internet, but I still don’t know what they’ll ask,” Lu Mingfei admitted.
“Well… different schools ask completely different questions. NYU and Harvard, for example, are nothing alike.”
“So which do you know better, Harvard or NYU?”
“Didn’t I tell you I entered the workforce right after high school?” Old Tang posted a dejected panda face.
“‘Entered the workforce’! Now that phrase shows real progress in your Chinese!”
“Enough, enough. Let’s video chat. I’ll coach your pronunciation,” Old Tang said.
Lu Mingfei glanced at Lu Mingze, asleep on the other bed, and hesitated. “Keep it down, then. My cousin’s sleeping.”
“No problem.”
The call beeped twice and connected. A cheerful-looking guy with drooping eyebrows waved from the window and thundered, “Hey! Bro!”
Lu Mingfei nearly lunged forward and swallowed the speakers.
“Quiet! Quiet!” Waving frantically at Old Tang, he unplugged them and connected his headset.
“What’s the big deal?” Old Tang muttered. “My place is right by the elevated tracks. It’s noisy here. Where are you, anyway? Why so careful?”
“I live with my uncle and aunt,” Lu Mingfei whispered.
“Oh, oh.” Old Tang nodded and lowered his voice, his Chinese sliding off-key. “So if this application works out, you can move out on your own? You should’ve said! Leave that interview to me!”
“You’re a real friend, Old Tang.” Lu Mingfei gave him a thumbs-up.
“As the number-one StarCraft player in the channel, if I don’t look out for number two, what kind of big brother am I?” Old Tang said. “Ha ha!”

For a moment, Lu Mingfei was touched. He felt a little more confident about tomorrow. He had drifted around all day, watched the sunset from the roof as usual, and still had no idea what to do. No one could tell him what an American college interview was like. The other applicants were probably having their pronunciation corrected word by word by tutors or parents. But Lu Mingfei had no one to help. After wandering around online for ages, he had happened to see Old Tang’s avatar bouncing and messaged him on the off chance. He didn’t even know Old Tang that well.
So there was someone, in some corner of the world he hadn’t thought of, who could help him after all. Someone with a baffling determination to play big brother and look after him.
Loyalty. This was loyalty!

“Come to think of it, I lost both my parents, too,” Old Tang went on with a sigh. “It’s hard getting by in America, you know, especially for people like us with both parents gone. At least I can get welfare…”
“Pah, pah, pah! Who lost both their parents? My mom and dad are just away from home!” Lu Mingfei spat furiously at him.
“Oh, oh. Saw-ree, saw-ree. Got the wrong end of the stick and the wrong end of the feelings.” Old Tang repeatedly clasped his hands in apology on the screen.
“Come on, man. Can you stop mangling Chinese? And what’s ‘saw-ree’? It’s ‘sorry,’ all right? Aren’t you supposed to be coaching my accent?” Lu Mingfei had no answer for his complete lack of a filter.

“Right, right. And once we’re done, we’ve got a few more matches to play. Come on, let’s start!” Old Tang cleared his throat. “The most common opening question is, why did you apply to our school? ‘Why did you apply this college, please show me some reason?’”
“But I didn’t apply…”
“Come on! No talking back. Repeat after me! I’m taking responsibility for your future, bro! ‘The great faculty is the key reason, and your college have very good research atmosphere…’”
“‘The great faculty is the key reason, and your college have very good research atmosphere…’” Lu Mingfei repeated each sound after Old Tang.

Night deepened. The small southern city grew still. Streetlights illuminated empty roads. Most apartment lights were out; only a few scattered windows remained bright. Behind one of them, a boy repeated the same sentences over and over in his indistinct pronunciation, cramming at the last minute. Tens of thousands of miles away, a guy eating yogurt shouted “No, no, no!” at every sound he got wrong.
Lu Mingze rolled his eyes, glanced at Lu Mingfei, grunted impatiently, stuffed both hands over his ears, and turned over.
The third morning. The Regent Hotel.

It was the most luxurious hotel in the city, part of a global five-star chain. Lu Mingfei knew the place because his uncle loved drinking tea and chatting with friends in its lobby, having the waiters refill the pot until the strong tea became plain water. It cost little that way, while allowing him the satisfaction of enjoying world-class service.
Lu Mingfei had never been through its glass doors. Now he looked around with eyes red from staying up all night.
This hotel is fucking luxurious! American schools are fucking rich! he marveled.

He sat outside a conference room on the executive floor. There were exactly seventeen chairs, one for each of the seventeen applicants. No one had asked for identification. As he had cautiously stepped through the hotel entrance, an attendant had smiled and asked, “Are you here for the Cassell College interview? Please follow me to the executive floor.” Then a pretty young woman in a skirt suit and ten-centimeter heels had led him to this room, where he found familiar faces.
Chen Wenwen, Su Xiaoqiang, Zhao Menghua, and Liu Miaomiao were all there. So were others from his school whose faces he knew but whose names he couldn’t remember, along with some he had never seen.
“Lu Mingfei?” Everyone who knew him sounded equally astonished, as though his presence here were an extraordinary event.
He could only wave the letter in his hand and grin. “I’m here for…” He swallowed. “…an interview, too.”
Then he slunk to the last chair. A form and a pencil lay on it. The form asked for his name, age, and similar details. He filled it in while his eyes darted around.

Things looked utterly hopeless. Everyone had prepared, and every one of them was formidable. Zhao Menghua’s pronunciation went without saying: his tutor was American. So did Su Xiaoqiang’s: she had spent a year in America during middle school. Even the usually casual Chen Wenwen had coordinated her outfit carefully: a navy skirt suit, white lace-edged socks, flat black shoes, and a white neck scarf. She had replaced her hair clip with one made of mother-of-pearl. She looked like one of those British aristocrats’ children in their school uniforms on television.
Lu Mingfei scratched his head and sighed.
“She looks so nice.” Having lost interest in comparing their chances, he turned to admire Chen Wenwen.

An attendant brought refreshments: a croissant and a glass of hot milk. Lu Mingfei ate the bread, drank the milk, and, with the problem of basic survival solved, went back to watching Chen Wenwen. After a while, a thought flashed through his head… What if a stroke of dumb luck got him through, and he could study abroad with her?
He looked up at the ceiling and suddenly gave two foolish chuckles, startling the people around him.
“Lu Mingfei, quiet. The interviewers are here. They’re inside.” Chen Wenwen covered her mouth as she whispered, pointing toward the inner conference room.
“Are you ready?” Beaming, he leaned over to make conversation. It was a pointless question. He only wanted to hear her speak.
“I’m not very confident.” Chen Wenwen glanced at Su Xiaoqiang and Zhao Menghua, then lowered her eyes, looking a little discouraged. “My spoken English isn’t as good as theirs…”
“You’ll be fine! I think your English is really…” Lu Mingfei began.

“Is Liu Miaomiao here?” The inner door opened and a tall, thin young man stepped out, speaking fluent Chinese and looking as unmistakably Chinese as anyone could. He wore a fitted dark-green suit, finely edged in silver at the collar. Gold buttons and cuffs gleamed, and a badge embroidered in silver thread rested on his chest. It looked like a school uniform, but Lu Mingfei had never seen one so exquisitely tailored.
The pretty pianist shot to her feet, her voice trembling slightly. “Here!”
“I’m Ye Sheng, one of your interviewers. Please come with me.” The young man smiled, showing white teeth.
Liu Miaomiao walked gracefully inside with Ye Sheng. The door closed. The sixteen people left outside looked at one another, none able to hide their nerves.

“Hey, did you look up this Cassell College’s website?” Zhao Menghua glanced at Su Xiaoqiang and Chen Wenwen, lowering his voice. “Apparently, it’s a really prestigious school. Lots of Harvard professors have gone over to teach there!”
“Yes.” Chen Wenwen nodded. “But I got an interview invitation without even applying.”
“Prestigious schools are like that, aren’t they? They don’t care about application fees. Just your ability,” Zhao Menghua said.
“If they only care about ability, how did someone like that sneak in?” Su Xiaoqiang gave Lu Mingfei a sidelong look.
Lu Mingfei shrugged his shoulders with the shameless indifference of someone who had nothing left to lose.
“I wonder how many they’ll admit,” Chen Wenwen whispered.
“One or two would be plenty!” Su Xiaoqiang said. “Haven’t you heard? Harvard only admits a few undergraduates from China each year.”

Lu Mingfei’s heart sank. He had no idea how many Chinese students Harvard admitted annually, but if there were only a handful in a country this huge, the odds of that particular stroke of dumb luck landing on him were microscopic. Eight-tenths of his hard-won confidence vanished.
“Well, I’m just here to try. I don’t have much hope,” Chen Wenwen said softly.
“None of us does,” Zhao Menghua said to comfort her.
“I don’t care.” Su Xiaoqiang was as haughty as ever. “If they don’t take me, I’ll go to Stanford. My dad has connections!”

The door opened, and Ye Sheng made a courteous gesture. Liu Miaomiao came out, turning back to thank him. She was clearly trying not to look disappointed, but the disappointment was written honestly across her face.
The pretty pianist hadn’t even lasted ten minutes! Her eyes a little red, Liu Miaomiao returned to her chair, took her bag, and headed straight out.
“Su Xiaoqiang,” Ye Sheng said.
The Little Celestial Princess sprang up, too, her lovely eyes wide, her teeth chattering.
Watching her follow Ye Sheng inside on stiff legs, Lu Mingfei let out a “Ha!”
“Don’t laugh at her. Aren’t you scared?” Chen Wenwen gave his shoulder a push.
“I’m not scared. What have I got to be scared of? I’m just here for the ride.” He laced his hands behind his head and sprawled across the chair.

When the Little Celestial Princess came out, her steps were stiffer than when she had gone in. Her expression was more angry than disappointed or dejected. Ye Sheng smiled politely behind her. She turned and shot him a furious look. Then he called Zhao Menghua inside.
“What kind of college is this? They’re making fools of us!” Su Xiaoqiang turned and left.
Lu Mingfei and Chen Wenwen exchanged a baffled look. The Little Celestial Princess had done worse than Liu Miaomiao. She had lasted perhaps five minutes.

Inside, the interviewer seemed less interested in conducting interviews than in practicing swordplay, cutting people down faster and faster. Zhao Menghua, reputed to have the best spoken English in the senior class, didn’t last even three minutes. When he was escorted out, his eyes were blank.
“Chen Wenwen,” Ye Sheng said.
“Good luck!” Lu Mingfei called softly after her.
She glanced back at him and nodded gently.

Seconds and minutes passed. Everyone outside remained silent. Lu Mingfei could hear his own heart pounding. He was a little afraid—afraid that Chen Wenwen would emerge with that same disappointed face.
She lasted fifteen minutes. When she came out, her face showed nothing. She kept her head down, looking at the tips of her shoes.
“How was it? How was it?” Lu Mingfei hurried over.
Chen Wenwen hesitated, then secretly beckoned him closer. “They’ll ask…”
Delighted, Lu Mingfei was just about to lean in when Ye Sheng said, “Lu Mingfei.”
He froze and turned. Ye Sheng was beckoning. “Lu Mingfei, you’re next.”
Strange. He had never met Ye Sheng. Had the man recognized him instantly from the tiny photograph on his University of Chicago application? Lu Mingfei was curious.

He followed Ye Sheng into the conference room. It was almost empty. At a vast table that could seat dozens sat just one girl, smiling sweetly. She wore the same uniform as Ye Sheng, only in a skirt suit, with a rose-red lace scarf tucked into her collar.
“My name is Aki Sakatoku. I’m also one of your interviewers.” The girl stood and bowed to Lu Mingfei in the unmistakably Japanese manner.
“Oh-high-yo.” Without thinking, Lu Mingfei bowed back.
After so many years shut away at home, playing countless PS2 games and watching endless anime, he did know a couple of lines of Japanese dialogue.
“Ohayō.” Aki Sakatoku covered her mouth and laughed softly, correcting the Henan accent he had somehow given his Japanese. Her smile had an older sister’s warmth.
Looks like I’ve made a good first impression, Lu Mingfei thought happily.
Ye Sheng sat beside Aki Sakatoku, opened his notebook, and looked at him. “Then let’s begin.”
Lu Mingfei nodded and took a deep breath, settling it deep in his belly. He had trained all night. Now came the test!
“Do you believe in aliens?” Aki Sakatoku asked gently.
He froze for an instant. Then he felt… a nuclear bomb go off inside his head… mushroom clouds everywhere, and nothing else at all.
What was happening? Surely the first question was supposed to be “Please introduce yourself” or “Why did you apply to our school?”
The answer to the first one was, “My name is Mingfei Lu, a Chinese high school student, I like online computer game and panda…”
The answer to the second was, “The great faculty is the key reason, and your college have very good research atmosphere…”
Old Tang had enthusiastically polished those answers. Lu Mingfei had then recited them seventy or eighty times before finally getting them down.
But this… What was this about aliens?
All that preparation… Completely useless!

Lu Mingfei’s eyes went as round as brass bells, and his head slowly drooped. This was the kind of loser he was. His luck was always spectacularly rotten. He was the guy who penciled a desk full of formulas before an exam, only for the teacher to make everyone swap seats; who finally managed a peek at the answer sheet next to him, only to discover that his neighbor had Test A and he had Test B… As a born loser, he should have had the courage to believe in his fate instead of putting up a pointless struggle.
“Sure. I believe in aliens,” he said. Suddenly, he felt Zhao Menghua was a hero for having lasted three minutes.
“Really?” Aki Sakatoku’s expression was mild, offering no sign of approval or disapproval. “Why do you believe in them?”

Hell, why did he believe? Believing was just believing. Nobody in the world could prove they had seen an alien, and yet some people believed and others didn’t. It was like asking why you liked the girl at the next desk in the white cotton dress. You could come up with thousands of reasons, but the real one was simply that you didn’t know what was happening: whenever you saw her, your heart raced; you cared terribly about what she said and remembered everything to do with her. And so you knew you liked her. Why? There was no reason, Lu Mingfei thought.
“I wander around on the roof at night a lot. Look at the stars when I’ve got nothing to do,” he said.
“Yes. Good. Looks at the stars in his spare time.” Aki Sakatoku took very earnest notes.
Lu Mingfei couldn’t understand her seriousness. You would have thought he was China’s foreign minister, solemnly delivering a mass of diplomatic language that needed to be carefully recorded.

“If you look at the stars, you start thinking. If there aren’t any aliens, the universe is so huge, tens of billions of light-years across, and a beam of light has to travel tens of billions of years to get from one end to the other, passing through so many galaxies. But the only time it meets people is here on Earth. It takes less than a second for light to pass Earth, so in tens of billions of years, there’s only one second when it encounters anyone. That would be the strange thing, wouldn’t it?” he said.
“Loneliness? Were you implying that the light is lonely?” Ye Sheng interjected.
Lu Mingfei scratched his head. He hadn’t actually been implying anything, but his answer seemed to have acquired a little depth. So he nodded, tacitly allowing Ye Sheng to see him as a lonely kid.
“Second question. Do you believe in superpowers?” Aki Sakatoku asked.
“Sure,” Lu Mingfei said. “Absolutely.”

Once he stopped caring, the questions weren’t difficult at all. If superpowers didn’t exist, then Jotaro Kujo’s Star Platinum wouldn’t exist, nor Luffy’s Gum-Gum Fruit, and Hiei’s Dragon of the Darkness Flame would naturally be fake, too. Then the main things left in the world would be the Montblanc watches his uncle never stopped mentioning and the soaring housing prices his aunt complained about more every day. His own future would be getting up every morning to catch a bus to work, paying the mortgage with his salary at the end of each month, and tiptoeing around his mother-in-law’s home on weekends, trying to please her… assuming any girl would marry him.
So in Lu Mingfei’s world, superpowers simply had to exist.
“And why do you believe in them?” Aki Sakatoku watched him with an encouraging smile.
“I believe… because I believe. Same as aliens,” he said.
He really couldn’t give her the actual reason. He could hardly say, “I love Jotaro Kujo’s Star Platinum, and I want it to be real.”
“A badass life needs no explanation,” Ye Sheng said.
Lu Mingfei stared. Why had the interviewer suddenly come out with an internet catchphrase?
He’s probably making fun of me, he thought.
“Third question. Do you think the foundation of human existence is idealist—mind and soul—or materialist—matter and the physical body?” Aki Sakatoku asked.
Lu Mingfei’s mind went blank on the spot.

Had these college interviewers fried their brains? Why was question three so different from the first two? This was high school politics class, wasn’t it? Analyzing materialism and idealism. But he had forgotten every bit of that after passing the graduation exam!
His face reddened, and he gulped air. Who knew how many people this question had taken down? But he had to get through it!
He let out a long breath, rolled his eyes, and stuck out his tongue.
“Er… what does sticking out your tongue mean?” Ye Sheng gave Aki Sakatoku a hesitant look.
“I don’t know.” Lu Mingfei sighed. “The question’s too deep. I really can’t answer it. Can I… give up?”
Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku were silent for a moment, then nodded. “Of course. Thank you for your interest in Cassell College.”
Ye Sheng stood. “I’ll show you out.”
Lu Mingfei had lasted one minute and thirty seconds, setting a new record for the quickest execution.
Chen Wenwen was waiting outside with her bag. Seeing him emerge, she hurried over. “Why are you out so soon?”
“The politics question got me…” His head drooped. “I’m not as good as you guys. How many did you answer?”
“The politics question got me, too. My answer was a mess. They said I hadn’t passed.” Chen Wenwen lowered her head.
“But you were in there fifteen minutes!” he said, startled.
“I talked about flying saucers for fifteen minutes…” she whispered.
“Huh?” He stared at her.

Then, in an instant, joy welled up inside him. He reached out and patted her head. “It’s fine, it’s fine! With questions from a bunch of lunatics like that, anyone who passed would have to be a lunatic, too!”
She raised her head, a hint of a smile appearing on her downcast face. Lu Mingfei’s heart bloomed. It felt like the greatest reward the day could have given him.
What did it matter if he couldn’t go abroad? Chen Wenwen wasn’t going either!
Late at night, Ye Sheng sat at the conference table, going through the applications once more.
He looked up at Aki Sakatoku beside him. “Where’s that little girl? Haven’t seen her all day. She didn’t even show up for the interviews. She’s supposed to be an interviewer, too.”
“Off having fun somewhere. That’s why she came along in the first place, isn’t it?” Aki Sakatoku shrugged. “What can you do? She’s still just a little girl.”
“How did the interviews go?” The door opened, and someone hurried in carrying a briefcase. “I booked a red-eye and came straight here after landing.”

It was an elderly man, travel-worn, with thick glasses perched on his nose. His gray hair was a fluffy mess, not because he had permed it, but because he hadn’t combed it in who knew how long. His suit was shabby, his trousers baggy.
“Professor Guderian.” Ye Sheng stood. “We interviewed seventeen students in all…”

“Don’t waste time! I’m asking about Lu Mingfei! I only care about Lu Mingfei!” Professor Guderian looked as anxious as a parent rather than an interviewer. “Tell me—how did he answer?” The old fellow of German descent spoke remarkably fluent Chinese.
Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku exchanged a glance. He turned to the page of notes on Lu Mingfei, hesitated, then shook his head.
“He left after just a minute and a half,” Ye Sheng said.
“The best students always hand in their papers first!” Professor Guderian was delighted.
“Well… for question one, he said he believed in aliens because without them, humanity would be rather lonely in the universe…” Ye Sheng smiled helplessly.
“What a wonderful answer! I’m genuinely moved!” Professor Guderian clicked his tongue in admiration. “That’s Lu Mingfei for you!”
“It… it’s that good?” Ye Sheng stared. “For question two, he believed in superpowers as well, but couldn’t give a reason…”
“Perfect!” Professor Guderian declared.
“That’s… a perfect answer? That’s the answer… the college had in mind?” Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku looked at one another.

“Let me explain!” Professor Guderian said. “In question one, not only did he say he believed in aliens, he introduced the crucial concept of loneliness. Loneliness is what binds our people together! That one word goes straight to the heart of the question. Aliens are a metaphor for the difference between our kind and ordinary people. For question two, belief requires absolutely no reason. What we mean by belief is an innate sense of trust that comes from within. If he had invented reasons for his trust, he would have lost points. How did he answer question three?”
“I don’t know…” Aki Sakatoku touched her forehead. “I mean, he said he didn’t know…”
Professor Guderian raised his head and drew a deep breath. “If I didn’t know how extraordinary his bloodline was, I’d think he’d peeked at the answers.”
“Don’t tell me the answer is… ‘I don’t know’?” Ye Sheng scratched his head.

“The answer is ‘I don’t know’! His bloodline determines his worldview. A person straddling two races also stands somewhere between idealism and materialism in his understanding of the world. That demonstrates his potential,” Professor Guderian said loudly. “Any student with real potential is bound to feel precisely that uncertainty about the world!”
“Professor Guderian, aren’t you simply… playing favorites?” Aki Sakatoku asked with a wry smile.
Professor Guderian paused, then spread his hands. “Well… a little… But I really do think he answered rather well…”

“I understand that the college makes allowances for students with exceptional bloodlines. But favoritism this blatant… isn’t it a bit much?” Ye Sheng shook his head. “If that’s how it is, why interview anyone at all?”
“You don’t understand. We haven’t had an S-rank candidate like this in decades. If we turn in an interview report that says he failed… the principal won’t let us off either!”
Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku exchanged a look. “He really is… S-rank?”

“Yes. It’s been checked again and again. Of all the candidates, he’s rated S. The only S! These interviews were, in fact, arranged for him alone!” Professor Guderian nodded and lowered his voice. “This is classified at the college’s highest level. That’s why you weren’t told before setting out.”
Silence.
“Ah!” Aki suddenly cried.
Professor Guderian clutched his chest. “Why are you shrieking all of a sudden?”
